hints: Focus on what NaOH(aq) under reflux does to a halogenoalkane, and what that tells you about the carbon skeleton of X.
Pentan-2-ol has the OH on carbon 2, so X must be 2-halopentan-2-yl type, that is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(Hal)CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.
Heating with KCN in ethanol just swaps the halogen for CN on that same carbon, so look for the nitrile with CN on carbon 2 of a five-carbon chain.
walkthrough:
**Recognise the first reaction**

Think like a detective. Aqueous NaOH heated under reflux converts a halogenoalkane to an alcohol by nucleophilic substitution.

$$\text{R-Hal} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{R-OH} + \text{Hal}^-$$

**Work backwards to find X**

The product is pentan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. The OH simply replaces where the halogen was.

So X must have the same five-carbon skeleton with Hal on carbon 2:
$$\text{X} = \text{CH}_3\text{CH(Hal)CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$$

**Apply the second reaction**

KCN in ethanol also does nucleophilic substitution, but $\text{CN}^-$ is the nucleophile.

$$\text{R-Hal} + \text{CN}^- \rightarrow \text{R-CN} + \text{Hal}^-$$
So we get the same skeleton with CN on carbon 2:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH(CN)CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$$
That is 2-cyanopentane, which matches the branched structure with CN on the second carbon.

options.A: This is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$, a straight-chain primary nitrile. It would come from 1-halopentane, which would give pentan-1-ol with NaOH(aq), not pentan-2-ol.
options.B: This is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CN)CH}_3$, a four-carbon chain with CN on carbon 2. It has only four carbons in the parent chain, so it cannot come from a five-carbon X. It is a trap for miscounting carbons.
options.C: This is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$, a six-carbon straight-chain nitrile. Substitution does not add extra carbons to the alkyl chain apart from the CN carbon itself, so this chain is too long.
options.D: This is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(CN)CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, with CN on carbon 2 of a five-carbon chain. It is exactly what you get when 2-halopentane undergoes substitution of Hal by CN, so it is correct.
